Past healthcare consolidations repeatedly drive up insurance premiums and prices while prioritizing corporate scale over patient affordability.

The $1 billion endowment commitment includes funding for healthcare disparities and research expansion.

[Source 1 — www.chicagotribune.com] (URL: https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/10/14/endeavor-health-rush-university-merger/?utm_campaign=mrf-bluesky-chicagotribune.com&utm_source=bluesky&utm_medium=social&mrfcid=202610156ac4724178bb54145cf65f1f):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Endeavor Health and Rush University System for Health announce plans to merge

A union between Endeavor Health and Rush University System for Health would create one of the largest health systems in Illinois.

Actual Article Body:
eNewspaper

Sign up for email newsletters

Sign up for email newsletters

eNewspaper

Trending:

Two major Chicago-area hospital systems — Endeavor Health and Rush University System for Health — announced plans Wednesday to merge, a union that would create one of the largest health systems in Illinois.

If the merger goes through, all the system’s hospitals would include “Rush” as part of their names, and the “Endeavor” name would eventually disappear.

Endeavor and Rush hope to close the deal in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. The combined system would include 12 hospitals, more than 46,000 employees and more than 400 sites of care.

The merger would allow Rush — which has three hospitals in Chicago, Aurora and Oak Park — to reach more patients in additional geographic areas, said Rush President and CEO Dr. Omar Lateef. He said he expects the merger would “dramatically improve care across the state of Illinois.”

It would also allow the nine-hospital Endeavor system to take advantage of Rush University Medical Center’s strong reputation as a premier academic medical institution. Rush University Medical Center tied with Northwestern Memorial Hospital for best hospital in the state this year in U.S. News & World Report’s annual rankings.

The systems’ leaders said they expect patients will have more access to care closer to home and clinical trials. The merged system would also likely open more outpatient sites, said Endeavor President and CEO J.P. Gallagher.

Endeavor now has hospitals in Evanston, Glenview, Highland Park, Skokie, Arlington Heights, Elmhurst, Naperville and Chicago.

When asked whether the merger would result in job losses or layoffs, Lateef said: “We’re doing this to grow and we want to grow our footprint. We want to grow in the state of Illinois. We expect jobs to increase.”

As part of the deal, Endeavor would put $1 billion from its endowment toward the new system’s efforts, including $300 million to reduce healthcare disparities in its communities; $500 million for Rush University to expand programs, research and clinical trials; and $200 million to improve quality and care.

Once the merger is completed, Gallagher would be named president and CEO of the system. Lateef, with Rush, had previously announced plans to retire from his leadership post in 2027. Lateef would stay in his current role through the close of the deal and then serve as CEO emeritus and as a strategic adviser to the CEO.

The deal must still get approval from state and federal regulators, who may look at it with an eye toward whether it would reduce competition and increase prices.

Some researchers have found that hospital consolidation results in higher prices for insurance companies, and those costs can be passed along to consumers through higher premiums and other payments. Hospitals have long disagreed with that notion, saying consolidations can lead to cost savings and higher quality of care.

“Hospital mergers are big corporate transactions that result in higher prices, service cuts, and other moves to maximize profits. The proposed merger of Rush and Endeavor is no different,” said Brenda Langford, a nurse at Stroger Hospital and a member of the National Nurses Organizing Committee board of directors, in a statement.

“Nurses call on state and federal regulators to block any merger that fails to guarantee all services are protected and nurses demand that we have a voice in the future of any merged health system,” Langford said.
Endeavor has been thwarted by federal regulators in the past. The Federal Trade Commission challenged a previous deal that would have merged NorthShore University HealthSystem, which is what Endeavor used to be called, and Advocate Health Care. The two systems walked away from that planned merger in 2017 after a federal judge ruled in favor of the FTC.

Gallagher, however, said Rush and Endeavor have already begun discussions with regulators and expects that “process to go smoothly.” He said he’s optimistic the deal will close in early 2027 as planned.

He also said that growing the system to increase leverage with insurers is not a driver of the merger, noting that many of the systems’ patients are on Medicare and Medicaid, which are government-funded health insurance programs.

“We’re confident that being able to do this at scale is based on being able to deliver care efficiently and in a way that is accessible and affordable,” Gallagher said.

He said a goal of the merger is to create a system that will be stable and strong over the long term.

The news of the merger follows the closures of West Suburban Medical Center in Oak Park and Weiss Memorial Hospital in Uptown. It also comes as a number of Chicago-area hospitals have cut their labor and delivery units, and others teeter on the brink of closure.

“As I think about some of the headlines that we’re seeing around healthcare in Chicago, they’re kind of sobering — hospitals shutting down, service lines getting limited,” Gallagher said. “This is us moving in an opposite direction.”

Endeavor and Rush are both in “a healthy situation today,” he said. Both organizations have had positive operating margins so far this year, according to financial statements.

Endeavor’s positive numbers, however, follow challenges.

Endeavor had operating losses of $494 million in 2024 and $33.9 million in 2025, according to financial statements. Much of the 2024 operating loss was attributable to $453 million in expenses to settle patients’ claims alleging one of Endeavor’s former doctors sexually abused them, Endeavor said in a financial disclosure in late 2024.

Gallagher said those earlier losses were not a motivation for the merger, and some of those losses were expected as Endeavor worked to integrate additional hospitals into its system.

Endeavor has been growing at a rapid pace in recent years — and if the merger is successful, this won’t be the first time it’s had to redo all of its signage.

Since 2020, back when it was still called NorthShore, the system has acquired Swedish Hospital in Chicago, Northwest Community Healthcare in Arlington Heights and merged with the system that was over Edward Hospital in Naperville, Elmhurst Hospital and Linden Oaks Behavioral Health.

After all that growth, NorthShore changed its name to Endeavor in late 2023.

For this new proposed merger, the leaders of the systems agreed that Rush would be the best name for the hospitals moving forward. The hospitals will keep their locations in their names.

“It’s been around for 150 years,” Gallagher said of Rush, “and as we thought about creating a singular organization, we felt it was important to make sure that that identity was also consistent.”

Endeavor first reached out to Rush in March about a potential merger, Gallagher said.

“I spoke with both CEOs and asked them those particular questions, and they assured me that they don’t have any plans for any layoffs, they don’t want to close any facilities, they actually think that the merger will allow them to cover even more territory and integrate some of their specialties without any layoffs,” Pritzker said.
The merger could allow Rush’s academic expertise to spread further through the Chicago area, said Daniel Hoang, a partner in consulting firm West Monroe’s healthcare practice, in an email.

“The question I’ll be watching is how they define success,” Hoang said. “Can they pair academic depth with local access and show measurable progress in care, workforce development and community health? If they can, this could offer a compelling model for how regional health systems grow.”

Such mergers are a way for hospital systems to bring together expertise, infrastructure and capabilities that might otherwise take years to develop on their own, he said.
The merger would place the new system among the largest in the state. Northwestern Medicine has 11 hospitals, Prime Healthcare has nine Illinois hospitals and Advocate Health Care has 11 hospitals, including its two-campus children’s hospital.

Chicago Tribune’s Dan Petrella contributed.

Former Apple engineers figured out how to get a biometric sensor to attach to your watch without any magnets or adhesives.

If you’re a watch enthusiast, you probably don’t want to exchange your prized timepiece for a bulky fitness tracker. But Hiyd founder Salah Batroukh doesn’t think people should have to sacrifice fashion for function.

“We don’t think that health tracking needs to be this overly conscious decision where you have to change something about the way you look,” Batroukh told TechCrunch. “That’s the ethos of the entire company. Our plan is to build out this product ecosystem of invisible health tracking.”

Hiyd’s first device to make health tracking look cooler is a small, slim disc that attaches to the back of your watch via microsuction, a material technology that allows the sensor to sit flush under your watch without magnets or adhesive. That way, it won’t leave any residue or mess with the mechanics of watches that keep time using magnets.

“Microsuction is essentially a textured silicone, with hundreds of tiny pockets per square inch molded into a pliable sheet. So when you press on it, it pushes air out of all those pockets, and you end up with a vacuum — just like traditional suction cups but scaled down incredibly,” Batroukh explained. “It works incredibly at stopping shear forces, but a little bit of prying allows it to pop right off, which is ideal for us. It’s also incredibly thin at just 0.3 mm with our manufacturing processes.”

According to Batroukh, the sensor, which measures 2.7 mm thick and weighs 7 grams, collects biometrics similar to those of leading wearables, including heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep staging, movement, calories burned, and VO2 max estimations, then syncs to an iOS or Android app. In order to fine-tune the sensor, Hiyd’s team is filming themselves doing various activities, then labeling those datasets to train its AI.

“We go for a walk and say, ‘This is somebody walking, this is somebody jogging, this is somebody running,’” he said. “The one thing that AI is really good at is data analysis, so we can basically fit a lot of heuristic analysis into our sets really quickly.”

On its app, Hiyd is also working to incorporate nutrition tracking. The goal isn’t to count calories, but rather to help users glean insights about how their eating habits impact their sleep quality or workout performance.

“What we will do is say like, ‘Hey, on days where you work out at 10 p.m. instead of 10 a.m., your sleep quality is actually worse,’ and that’ll be specific to you,” he said. “Or it’ll say, ‘Hey, we think you had a less deep sleep last night because you had a slice of cake before you went to bed, and the sugar affected it.’”

Batroukh spent about seven years as a manufacturing design engineer at Apple, a company synonymous with iconic hardware. But he wanted to know if he could design something great without the support of a global brand and a multitrillion-dollar market cap.

“One of the reasons I left Apple was a lot of the products became a little bit more about being an Apple product, rather than being something for the customer,” he said. “[Hiyd] gives me the opportunity to do the exact opposite.”

Batroukh is joined by fellow founders Omar Shakir, an experienced mechanical engineer who is the startup’s CTO, and Mahamad Charawi, who is its head of software. (Charawi previously co-led the Y Combinator-backed startup Laudspeaker through its sale.)

Hiyd is bringing its tiny sensor to the big stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, where the company is competing as one of the top 20 companies at Startup Battlefield on Wednesday. (Don’t miss out on the action.) In November, the company plans to launch a Kickstarter. So far, over 16,000 people have made deposits to secure Hiyd’s first units.
